description: 🦅 Equipo 100% virtual de Piura. Lidera Jhonny Ramírez Chiroque, dev Senior (cloud Azure, backend, APIs). Reto base: Field Shift (datos NASA para el agro de Piura); también evaluamos otros retos. Buscamos UX-UI/frontend, datos/GIS, ciencias o arte digital. ¡No necesitas programar! Virtual team, all backgrounds welcome!
summary: AllpaShift is a web and mobile app (Android and iOS) that turns NASA Earth observations into simple farming decisions: what to plant, when to plant it, and what to change when extreme weather is coming. A farmer picks a plot on a risk map and gets one clear action for the next two weeks, the month-by-month risk of the season (drought, extreme rain, heat, frost and El Niño) and three crop rotations, including the usual one. Each rotation gets a climate score, a soil-health score (legumes, crop families, root depth, soil cover, bare months, monoculture, salinity) and a water score, weighted by the farmer's priority and the irrigation water they have. Every rotation lists its benefits, risks, unknowns and what to check with a local expert. AllpaShift combines six NASA datasets: POWER, GPM IMERG (monthly and daily), SMAP soil moisture, MODIS NDVI vegetation and MUR SST sea temperature, the early El Niño signal. All calculations use transparent rules; an open AI model only explains results in plain words. Applied to real 2017 data, AllpaShift would have warned Piura farmers weeks before the coastal El Niño rains. We don't predict the weather. We prepare farmers, and their soil, for it.
details:
What does it do?

AllpaShift helps small farmers decide what to plant, when to plant it and what to change when extreme weather is coming. The farmer picks a plot on a map (or uses the phone's GPS), marks the soil type and salinity (the app suggests the soil type, organic matter and infiltration from SoilGrids), chooses what matters most (take less risk, save water or care for the soil), says how much irrigation water they have, and can test a dry or wet year. The app answers in plain language:

  • What to do now: one action for this fortnight (plant, wait, irrigate, protect or prepare drainage), with the best rotation and its climate, soil and water scores right on the home screen.
  • Season risk: month-by-month risk from planting to harvest against drought, extreme rain, heat, frost and El Niño, with the crop's water demand (reference evapotranspiration, FAO-56).
  • What to change: three crop rotations, always including the usual one in the valley (e.g. rice after rice), compared by a climate score, a soil-health score and a water score, and a final score weighted by the farmer's priority. The app says why the recommended rotation was chosen.
  • Before you decide: for each rotation, its benefits, risks and trade-offs, what we don't know (uncertainty) and what to check with a local expert (market, pests, water, seed).
  • Would it have worked? A "time machine" applies today's rules to real data from 2001 to 2026. In 2017 AllpaShift would have raised the first El Niño warning 12 weeks, and the "prepare drainage" alert 6 weeks, before the peak rains. Tapping any month shows its rain day by day and week by week.

How does it work?

  1. The app (web, Android or iOS) calls the AllpaShift API (Java, Spring Boot). The API answers from its PostgreSQL database when the result is fresh, so the tool keeps working even if a NASA server is slow.
  2. Otherwise, a Python calculation service reads NASA data for that point: POWER (temperature, rainfall, climatology), GPM IMERG (satellite rainfall), SMAP (soil moisture), MODIS NDVI (crop vigor) and MUR SST (sea temperature, Niño 1+2).
  3. Each indicator is compared with its normal and gets a level: low, medium or high. Season risk adds frost (normal minimum of 2 °C or less) and evapotranspiration.
  4. Climate score: each rotation starts at 100 and loses points for water needs versus deficit, months outside the crop's temperature range, high-risk months and planting out of season.
  5. Soil-health score: nitrogen-fixing legumes, alternating root depths and soil cover add points; monoculture, two crops of the same family, two water-hungry crops in a row, three or more months of bare soil, and salt-sensitive crops on saline soil lose points. Crop traits come from FAO-56 and FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29.
  6. Water score depends on the crops' water use and the irrigation water the farmer has. The final score combines climate, soil and water with weights set by the farmer's priority. Every point gained or lost is shown with its reason and source.
  7. The API stores the result and every NASA value used. If a value is missing, the app says "no data"; it never invents values.

Benefits and impact

Farmers move from planting by habit to planting with data, reduce losses from drought, floods, heat and frost, save water, and choose rotations that rebuild the soil. NASA data becomes understandable for people without technical training, in English and Spanish.

What makes it creative?

It combines sea temperature as an early El Niño signal with satellite rain, soil moisture and vegetation in one simple decision; it puts the farmer's own soil, water and priority inside the score; it is honest about what it doesn't know; and it proves itself against the real 2017 disaster instead of only promising.

Tools and languages

Vue 3, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Chart.js and Capacitor (web, Android, iOS); Java 17 with Spring Boot and Spring Cloud Gateway; Python with FastAPI, pandas and pytest; PostgreSQL; Docker and Nginx on a cloud server; NASA POWER API, NASA Earthdata (CMR, OPeNDAP), ORNL DAAC MODIS web service, NOAA ERDDAP; SoilGrids REST API (ISRIC); Groq with the open model gpt-oss-20b (Apache 2.0) for explanations only; GitHub. Code under Apache 2.0. Live app: https://allpashift.crisaor.org

Factors we considered

Honesty: every value shows the dataset it really comes from; soil data is labelled as SoilGrids or "data you gave", never as NASA data; missing data is shown as "no data". Transparency: rules and thresholds live in configuration files and are covered by automated tests (138 in Python, 43 in Java). Reliability: results are stored in the database, so the tool keeps working when external servers are slow. Accessibility: plain language, English and Spanish, mobile-first design for the field. AllpaShift supports decisions; it does not replace the judgment of farmers or local agricultural experts.
